blocks.text: Jaccard similarity answers a deceptively simple question: given two collections of distinct items, how much do they overlap, relative to how much ground they cover between them. Unlike the Geometry module's Euclidean, Manhattan, and cosine similarity lessons, which all compare numeric vectors, Jaccard similarity compares sets directly, making it the natural tool whenever the objects being compared are collections of tags, words, categories, or IDs rather than points in a coordinate space.

1. What Jaccard Similarity Measures

Jaccard similarity measures how similar two sets are by comparing what they share against everything they contain in total. Formally, it is the size of the intersection of two sets divided by the size of their union. If two sets share every element and contain nothing else, their Jaccard similarity is 1. If they share nothing at all, it is 0.

This makes Jaccard similarity a pure measure of overlap that completely ignores order, count, and any notion of numeric distance between elements. Two sets of tags such as {"python", "backend", "api"} and {"python", "api", "database"} are compared purely on which tags are shared and which are not, with no concept of one tag being "closer" to another.

blocks.title: Similarity between collections, not points
blocks.content: Jaccard similarity does not operate on coordinates or embeddings at all. It operates directly on sets of discrete items, such as words, tags, categories, or user IDs, where the only question that matters is membership: is this item in the set or not.

blocks.text: 1.1 A Non-Numeric Example

Consider two GitHub repositories compared by the set of programming languages each one uses. One repository uses {"Python", "SQL"} and another uses {"Python", "SQL", "JavaScript"}. Neither set contains anything that could meaningfully be treated as a coordinate or magnitude, yet Jaccard similarity compares them cleanly: the shared languages divided by all languages used across both, no numeric encoding required.
2. Why Sets, Not Vectors

Many similarity measures, including everything covered in the Geometry module, treat data as vectors: ordered lists of numbers living in a coordinate space, where distance and angle carry meaning. A great deal of real data, however, is naturally unordered and non-numeric: the set of tags attached to an article, the set of products a customer purchased, the set of words appearing in a document, the set of users who liked a particular post.

Forcing this kind of data into a numeric vector is possible, for example by one-hot encoding every possible tag into a 0 or 1 column, but Jaccard similarity skips that conversion entirely and compares the underlying sets directly. This makes it simpler to reason about and cheaper to compute when the universe of possible items is large but any single set only contains a small handful of them.
2.1 A Concrete Contrast

Consider comparing two products by the set of categories each belongs to, versus comparing two products by a numeric feature vector of price, weight, and rating. The categories comparison is naturally a set question, best answered with Jaccard similarity; the numeric feature comparison is naturally a vector question, best answered with Euclidean or cosine similarity from the Geometry module.
3. The Jaccard Similarity Formula

For two sets A and B, Jaccard similarity is defined as the number of elements in both A and B, divided by the number of elements in either A or B (or both). Written with set notation, it is the size of A intersect B, divided by the size of A union B.

code.content:
Jaccard similarity formula:

J(A, B) = |A intersect B| / |A union B|

where:
  A intersect B  is the set of elements present in BOTH A and B
  A union B      is the set of all elements present in A, B, or both
  |S|            denotes the number of elements (the size) of set S

blocks.text: Because the union always contains at least as many elements as the intersection, the ratio is always between 0 and 1 inclusive. A ratio of 1 means the two sets are identical; a ratio of 0 means the two sets share nothing at all, that is, their intersection is empty.
3.1 An Equivalent Way to Write the Formula

The union size can also be written as the size of A, plus the size of B, minus the size of the intersection, since simply adding |A| and |B| double counts every shared element once. This gives an equivalent, sometimes more convenient, formula: J(A, B) equals |A intersect B| divided by (|A| plus |B| minus |A intersect B|), useful when a system already tracks the sizes of A and B and only needs to additionally compute the intersection size.
4. Jaccard Distance

Jaccard distance converts the similarity score into a dissimilarity score, defined simply as 1 minus Jaccard similarity. Where Jaccard similarity of 1 means identical sets, Jaccard distance of 0 means identical sets, following the usual convention that a distance of 0 means no difference at all.

code.content:
Jaccard distance formula:

d_J(A, B) = 1 - J(A, B) = 1 - |A intersect B| / |A union B|

blocks.text: Jaccard distance is a true mathematical distance metric, satisfying the triangle inequality, which makes it usable in algorithms that expect a proper distance function, such as certain clustering methods that need to compare how far apart two sets of items are rather than how similar they are.
5. Properties of Jaccard Similarity

A handful of properties make Jaccard similarity predictable and easy to reason about. It is symmetric, meaning J(A, B) always equals J(B, A), since intersection and union do not care about the order their two arguments are given in. It always falls strictly within the closed range from 0 to 1.

It equals exactly 1 only when the two sets are identical, and it equals exactly 0 only when the two sets share no elements whatsoever. Duplicate elements within a single set are irrelevant, since sets by definition only track distinct membership, not counts, which is an important distinction from techniques that do care about how many times an item appears.

blocks.text: 5.1 Jaccard Similarity Is Not Defined for Multisets by Default

Standard Jaccard similarity treats its inputs strictly as sets, meaning repeated elements collapse to a single membership flag. If counts genuinely matter, for example comparing two shopping carts where buying an item three times should count differently than buying it once, a related measure called the Jaccard index for multisets, or weighted Jaccard similarity, generalizes the formula using minimum and maximum counts per element instead of plain set membership.
6. Implementing Jaccard Similarity in Code

Because Python sets already support intersection and union directly, implementing Jaccard similarity is a short, direct translation of the formula, with one small guard needed for the edge case where both input sets are empty, which would otherwise divide by zero.
6.1 Handling Very Large Sets

For sets containing millions of elements, computing an exact intersection and union can become expensive. In those situations, an approximation technique called MinHash is commonly used to estimate Jaccard similarity far more cheaply, which is revisited briefly later in this lesson and covered more fully alongside hashing based approximate methods.
7. Contrasting Jaccard Similarity with Vector-Based Metrics

The Geometry module's Euclidean, Manhattan, and cosine similarity lessons all assume the inputs are numeric vectors of the same fixed length and dimension, where each position means the same thing across every vector being compared. Jaccard similarity makes no such assumption: the two sets being compared can have completely different sizes, and there is no notion of a shared coordinate axis.

This leads to a simple rule of thumb: reach for cosine similarity or Euclidean distance when comparing dense numeric representations such as embeddings, and reach for Jaccard similarity when comparing raw collections of discrete items such as tags, categories, or purchased product IDs, where converting to a numeric vector would be an unnecessary detour.

blocks.text: 8. AI Relevance: Comparing Sets of Recommended Items

Recommendation systems frequently need to compare two users, two sessions, or two model versions by the set of items each one recommends or interacts with. Jaccard similarity gives a simple, interpretable score for how much two recommendation lists overlap, without needing any numeric embedding of the items involved.

A common use is comparing the top-K recommended items produced by two different model versions during an evaluation, or comparing which items two similar users both purchased, as a lightweight signal for user-based collaborative filtering, where a high Jaccard similarity between two users' purchase sets suggests they may enjoy similar future recommendations.
9. AI Relevance: Document Similarity via Shared Word Sets

Treating each document as the set of distinct words, or the set of distinct short phrases called shingles, that appear in it turns document similarity into a Jaccard similarity computation. Two news articles covering the same event tend to share a large fraction of their distinct vocabulary, giving them a high Jaccard similarity, while two unrelated articles share very little.

This set based approach to text is coarser than modern embedding based similarity, since it ignores word order, meaning, and synonyms entirely, but it remains useful precisely because it is cheap, requires no trained model, and gives an easily explainable score: "these two documents share 40 percent of their distinct words."
9.1 Shingles Instead of Whole Words

Rather than splitting a document into individual words, many implementations split it into overlapping sequences of a few consecutive words or characters, called shingles or n-grams. Comparing documents through their sets of shingles rather than their sets of whole words captures some local word order information, since a shared 3-word shingle is stronger evidence of real overlap than two documents merely sharing common individual words like "the" or "data".
10. AI Relevance: Deduplication of Near-Identical Records

Data pipelines frequently contain near-duplicate records, such as two customer entries that differ only by a typo, or two scraped web pages that are copies of each other with minor formatting differences. Representing each record as a set of tokens, such as words or character shingles, and computing Jaccard similarity between records is a standard way to flag likely duplicates without requiring an exact string match.

A typical deduplication pipeline sets a similarity threshold, for example flagging any pair of records with Jaccard similarity above 0.8 as likely duplicates for manual review or automatic merging. This threshold based approach tolerates small differences, like a reordered word or a minor spelling variation, that an exact string comparison would incorrectly treat as completely different records.
10.1 Choosing a Similarity Threshold

The right Jaccard similarity threshold for flagging duplicates depends entirely on the data and the cost of each type of mistake. A threshold set too low risks merging genuinely distinct records that happen to share some common tokens; a threshold set too high risks missing true duplicates that differ by more than a trivial amount. Teams typically tune this threshold empirically against a small hand-labeled sample of known duplicate and non-duplicate pairs.
11. Scaling Jaccard Similarity to Huge Collections: MinHash

Computing exact Jaccard similarity requires building the full intersection and union of two sets, which becomes slow when comparing millions of pairs of large sets, such as deduplicating an entire web scale document collection against itself. MinHash is a hashing based technique that estimates Jaccard similarity approximately, using a small fixed size signature per set instead of the full set, dramatically reducing both memory and comparison cost.

The core idea previews a theme that returns in the hashing lesson of the ann-search-mathematics module: instead of comparing full objects directly, compress each one down to a compact signature such that similar objects are likely to produce similar or matching signatures, then compare the cheap signatures instead of the expensive originals.
12. Worked Example: Two Sets of Tags

Consider two articles tagged by an editorial system. Article A carries the tags {"machine learning", "python", "tutorial", "beginner"}. Article B carries the tags {"machine learning", "python", "advanced", "deployment"}.
12.1 Computing the Intersection and Union

The intersection, the tags present in both articles, is {"machine learning", "python"}, which has 2 elements. The union, every distinct tag appearing in either article, is {"machine learning", "python", "tutorial", "beginner", "advanced", "deployment"}, which has 6 elements.

blocks.text: Jaccard similarity is therefore 2 divided by 6, which equals approximately 0.333. Jaccard distance is 1 minus 0.333, which equals approximately 0.667. In plain terms, the two articles share about a third of their combined distinct tags, suggesting moderate but not strong topical overlap.
13. Common Mistakes

items: Passing in lists with duplicate elements and expecting duplicates to increase the similarity score, when Jaccard similarity only ever considers distinct set membership.

Applying Jaccard similarity to numeric feature vectors directly, when the data is really continuous and a vector based measure like cosine or Euclidean distance from the Geometry module is more appropriate.
Forgetting the empty set edge case, where both sets being compared are empty, which naively divides zero by zero unless handled explicitly.
Assuming a low Jaccard similarity between two documents means they are unrelated in meaning, when it may only mean they use different specific vocabulary to discuss the same topic.
Computing exact Jaccard similarity over millions of large sets without considering MinHash or another approximation, leading to unnecessarily slow pipelines.

blocks.text: 14. Practice: Compare Two Customer Purchase Sets

An e-commerce system wants to check whether two customers have similar taste, using the set of distinct product categories each customer has purchased from. Customer 1 has purchased from categories {"electronics", "books", "home", "fitness"}. Customer 2 has purchased from categories {"books", "fitness", "outdoors"}.

As a check on your work: the intersection here is {"books", "fitness"}, size 2, and the union is {"electronics", "books", "home", "fitness", "outdoors"}, size 5, giving a Jaccard similarity of 0.4 exactly, right at the threshold in this example.
Key Takeaway

Jaccard similarity measures overlap between two sets as the size of their shared elements divided by the size of everything they contain combined, giving a score between 0 and 1 that needs no numeric vector representation at all. It complements, rather than replaces, the vector based metrics from the Geometry module, and is the natural choice whenever the underlying data is a collection of discrete items such as tags, words, or IDs.

In AI systems, Jaccard similarity shows up quietly and constantly: comparing recommended item sets, measuring document overlap through shared vocabulary, and flagging near-duplicate records during data cleaning, and for very large collections its ideas extend naturally into hashing based approximations like MinHash covered later in this curriculum.
